title: The Copper Clock
premise: In 1913, Odile Lockridge drives for the suffragist Mrs. Halloway and secretly reads every letter that passes through their hands, learning the town's secrets to decide which silences keep people safe. When the river bridge closes for winter repairs, the isolated household becomes a pressure cooker: a fugitive suffragist arrives wounded, a letter Odile never delivered resurfaces, and word comes that only one berth remains on the last ferry south before ice. Forced to choose which member of her found family escapes the coming crackdown — and to confess five years of opened letters — Odile discovers that belonging means being known, not protected. The book ends with Odile staying behind as the others cross, choosing the family she built over the safety she could have taken.
about_author: Oscar Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing private correspondence in provincial collections. They write historical fiction about the small betrayals and loyalties preserved in other people's letters.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sealed Paper
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She steams open the morning post in the carriage house, introducing her ritual of reading before delivering, and the household she serves: Mrs. Halloway, the cook Bess, and young apprentice Tom. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking loneliness; Odile believes knowledge is how she earns her place.

chapters.title: Five Years of Other People's Words
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present-day errands: how Odile came to the Halloway house after her own family cast her out, and the first letter she read — one that saved Mrs. Halloway from an informer. POV alternates Odile and Bess. Beat: the origin of Odile's creed that silence can be protection.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Town criers announce the river bridge will shut for winter repairs; the last crossing is in six weeks. Odile's POV as supplies are hoarded and letters pile up undeliverable. Beat: dread — the house is now sealed inside its own secrets with no road out.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Mill Gate
chapters.summary: Bess's POV. A wounded woman, Clara Voss, arrives claiming Mrs. Halloway sent for her; she carries a warrant notice in her coat. Odile reads it before anyone else sees it. Beat: fear and fascination — Odile must decide whether this secret belongs in her keeping.

chapters.title: What the Letters Never Said
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway's POV. She reveals she has always known Odile reads the mail — and approves. A fragile intimacy forms between mistress and driver. Beat: relief curdling into unease; being seen is not the same as being safe.

chapters.title: Tom Learns to Listen
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. The apprentice catches Odile with a half-opened letter and, instead of exposing her, asks to be taught. Beat: warmth and mentorship — the found family quietly grows, and so does the circle of shared risk.

chapters.title: The Undelivered Letter
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Among the backlog she finds a letter she intercepted years ago — from Mrs. Halloway's estranged daughter — and never delivered. Clara's arrival makes the old omission impossible to hide. Beat: guilt surfacing; Odile's protective silences begin to look like thefts.

chapters.title: Ice on the River
chapters.summary: Bess's POV. Winter tightens; food runs short; townsfolk whisper about the 'seditious women' shut in past the mill. A constable comes asking questions. Beat: external threat crystallizes — the closed bridge protects them from nothing.

chapters.title: Clara's Testimony
chapters.summary: Clara's POV, told by firelight: prison, force-feeding, the friend who didn't survive. Tom listens; Bess weeps; Odile takes notes for a pamphlet. Beat: grief transformed into purpose — the household becomes a movement, not just a refuge.

chapters.title: The Ferry Notice
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A smuggled message: one berth remains on the final ferry south before the channel ices — enough papers and money for exactly one person to escape the warrants. Beat: hope arriving as arithmetic; someone must be left behind.

chapters.title: Everyone Volunteers
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, rotating short POVs (Tom, Bess, Clara). Each argues they should stay: Tom because he's least known, Bess because the house needs her, Clara because she's already condemned. Beat: love expressed as self-sacrifice; the choice grows heavier the kinder they all are.

chapters.title: Mrs. Halloway Decides
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway's POV. She names herself — she is the symbol; her capture would be worth ten escapes. Odile, alone among them, knows from five years of letters that the authorities want her alive and talking. Beat: Odile's knowledge becomes a burden she cannot ethically keep silent.

chapters.title: Confession at the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She confesses everything: every letter read, every secret kept, including the daughter's letter still hidden in her trunk. Beat: the novel's moral pivot — trust shattered and rebuilt in a single scene; the family must decide if knowing everything destroys them.

chapters.title: The Daughter's Reply
chapters.summary: Bess's POV. Against Odile's advice, they finally open the daughter's letter: it is not angry but pleading — she has been searching for her mother for three years. Beat: devastating tenderness; Odile's oldest silence cost the most.

chapters.title: The Constable Returns
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. The constable returns with a search order effective when the thaw comes — weeks away, but certain. He hints he can be bought. Beat: ticking clock made explicit; the ferry berth is now not an opportunity but a countdown.

chapters.title: Bargaining with a Small Man
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She meets the constable privately, using what she knows from letters to leverage his silence — and learns he wants the berth himself, for his own son. Beat: moral compromise; Odile recognizes her own methods turned against her.

chapters.title: Which Silence Keeps Who Safe
chapters.summary: Clara's POV. Clara confronts Odile: your reading kept us safe or kept us small? The household votes on who takes the berth. Beat: rising tension peaks — the vote deadlocks between Mrs. Halloway and Clara, and Odile holds the deciding voice.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, climax. At the frozen dock she gives the berth to Clara — the one whose life is most immediately forfeit — and hands Mrs. Halloway the daughter's address instead. Beat: climax and sacrifice; Odile chooses repair over rescue, connection over escape.

chapters.title: Crossing
chapters.summary: Clara's POV aboard the ferry, watching the shore recede, carrying the household's letters and the pamphlet manuscript. Beat: bittersweet release; survival framed as responsibility to those left behind.

chapters.title: The Long Thaw
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Winter in the sealed house: rationed bread, taught letters, Tom printing pamphlets on the kitchen press. The constable, paid in secrets, looks away. Beat: quiet resilience; the found family endures without the person they freed.

chapters.title: The Bridge Opens
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway's POV. Spring: the bridge reopens, and the first traveler across is the daughter, come at last to the door. Mother and Odile meet her together, all secrets spent. Beat: reconciliation earned through honesty rather than protection.

chapters.title: Letters We Sign Our Names To
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, epilogue. She delivers mail openly now, unsealed by agreement; the household writes to Clara under false names that everyone knows. Final beat: belonging redefined — a family is not what you protect people from, but what you let them know.
